walkthroughs.body_html:
Cell Division & Genetics — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Cell Division & Genetics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Cell Division & Genetics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why must DNA replicate before mitosis?
options: To save energy
So each daughter cell gets a complete set
To form new chromosomes
To make ATP

mcqs.q: What is the key difference between mitosis and meiosis?
options: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells; meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells (gametes).
Mitosis happens in plants and meiosis happens in animals.
Mitosis and meiosis both produce gametes; they are basically the same.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: What is the key structural difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Mitosis happens in plants and meiosis happens in animals.
Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes do not.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
Prokaryotes have no DNA — that's why they have no nucleus.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
Mitosis happens in plants and meiosis happens in animals.
